questions.question: At which OSI layer does the Application Load Balancer (ALB) operate?

options.text: Layer 3 (Network)
Layer 4 (Transport)
Layer 7 (Application)
Layer 2 (Data Link)

explanation.correct: ALB operates at Layer 7 (Application Layer), which allows it to inspect the full HTTP request including path, headers, and query strings.
explanation.why: Layer 4 is the Network Load Balancer (NLB). Layer 3 is the Gateway Load Balancer. Layer 2 is the Data Link layer not used for load balancers.

questions.question: At which OSI layer does the Network Load Balancer (NLB) operate?

options.text: Layer 7 (Application)
Layer 4 (Transport)
Layer 5 (Session)
Layer 3 (Network)

explanation.correct: NLB operates at Layer 4 (Transport Layer), routing traffic based only on IP address and TCP/UDP port number.
explanation.why: Layer 7 is ALB. NLB does not inspect HTTP content. It works at the transport layer with TCP and UDP protocols.

questions.question: What is the primary basis for path-based routing in an ALB?

options.text: IP address of the client
TCP port number
URL path of the HTTP request
Source MAC address

explanation.correct: ALB path-based routing uses the URL path (e.g., /products, /cart, /orders) to determine which target group receives the request.
explanation.why: IP-based and port-based routing is done by NLB. MAC addresses are a Layer 2 concept and not used by load balancers.

questions.question: What is a Target Group in the context of an ALB?

options.text: A group of load balancers
A logical grouping of backend resources that receive forwarded traffic
A set of CloudWatch alarms
A collection of IAM roles

explanation.correct: A target group is a logical grouping of backend resources (EC2 instances, IPs, or Lambda functions) that the ALB routes traffic to.
explanation.why: Load balancers are not grouped into target groups. CloudWatch alarms are separate monitoring resources. IAM roles are security constructs.

questions.question: What does an ALB return to a client if all instances in the target group fail their health checks?

options.text: 200 OK
404 Not Found
503 Service Unavailable
500 Internal Server Error

explanation.correct: When no healthy targets exist in a target group, the ALB returns a 503 Service Unavailable error to the client.
explanation.why: 200 means success. 404 means the resource was not found. 500 is a generic server error. 503 specifically means the service is temporarily unavailable — which is what happens when no healthy targets exist.

questions.question: What is a Launch Template in the context of Auto Scaling Groups?

options.text: A CloudFormation template for deploying applications
A blueprint defining the configuration for new EC2 instances launched by the ASG
A set of IAM policies for EC2 access
An S3 bucket policy template

explanation.correct: A Launch Template defines the AMI, instance type, key pair, security groups, and user data used when ASG automatically launches new EC2 instances.
explanation.why: CloudFormation templates deploy infrastructure stacks. IAM policies control permissions. S3 bucket policies control access — none of these define EC2 instance configuration for ASG.

questions.question: Which of the following is the 'floor' capacity setting in an Auto Scaling Group?

options.text: Desired capacity
Maximum capacity
Minimum capacity
Target capacity

explanation.correct: Minimum capacity is the floor — the ASG will never scale below this number of instances, even during very low demand periods.
explanation.why: Desired is the current target. Maximum is the ceiling. There is no 'target capacity' setting — that term relates to target tracking policy metrics.

questions.question: Which load balancer supports Elastic IP (static IP) addresses?

options.text: Application Load Balancer (ALB)
Network Load Balancer (NLB)
Both ALB and NLB
Neither — ELB only uses DNS names

explanation.correct: NLB supports Elastic IP addresses (static IPs), making it suitable for use cases where clients need to whitelist a specific IP address.
explanation.why: ALB only provides a DNS name with dynamic IP addresses that can change. NLB's static IP support is a key differentiating feature.

questions.question: What happens when an Auto Scaling Group launches a new EC2 instance and the ASG is attached to an ALB target group?

options.text: You must manually register the new instance with the target group
The new instance is automatically registered with the target group
A new target group is created for the instance
The load balancer restarts to include the new instance

explanation.correct: When an ASG is attached to a target group, new instances launched by the ASG are automatically registered with the target group. The ALB begins routing traffic once health checks pass.
explanation.why: Manual registration defeats the purpose of Auto Scaling. No new target group is created. The load balancer does not restart — it dynamically updates its target list.

questions.question: Which of the following routing capabilities is EXCLUSIVE to the Application Load Balancer and NOT available in the Network Load Balancer?

options.text: Routing by IP address
Routing by TCP port
Routing by URL path and HTTP headers
Distributing traffic across multiple instances

explanation.correct: ALB can route based on URL path, HTTP headers, query strings, and HTTP method because it operates at Layer 7 and understands HTTP. NLB only sees IP and port.
explanation.why: Both ALB and NLB route by IP and TCP port. Both distribute traffic across multiple instances. Only ALB, as a Layer 7 balancer, can inspect and route based on HTTP content.

questions.question: Your e-commerce application has separate microservices for /products, /cart, and /orders. Which AWS service enables a SINGLE entry point to route traffic to all three services based on the URL?

options.text: Network Load Balancer with three listeners
Route 53 with weighted routing
Application Load Balancer with path-based routing rules
API Gateway with three separate APIs

explanation.correct: ALB path-based routing is the designed solution for this pattern. A single ALB listener with path-based rules routes /products, /cart, and /orders to their respective target groups.
explanation.why: NLB cannot route by URL path (Layer 4 only). Route 53 distributes DNS queries, not HTTP paths. API Gateway is a valid option but the session specifically covered ALB for this use case.

questions.question: What is the role of an ALB Listener?

options.text: It performs health checks on EC2 instances
It monitors CloudWatch metrics for the load balancer
It checks for incoming connection requests using a configured protocol and port
It registers EC2 instances with the load balancer

explanation.correct: A listener is a process configured on the ALB with a protocol (HTTP/HTTPS) and port (80/443) that checks for incoming connection requests and applies routing rules.
explanation.why: Health checks are a target group function. CloudWatch monitoring is separate. Instance registration is handled by the target group and ASG integration.

questions.question: A company needs to direct mobile users to a different backend than desktop users using their existing load balancer. Which load balancer type supports this and what feature would you use?

options.text: NLB using port-based routing
ALB using HTTP header-based routing rules
NLB using IP-based routing
ALB using IP address rules

explanation.correct: ALB supports routing based on HTTP headers including User-Agent, which identifies mobile vs desktop browsers. You create a listener rule with a header condition to route mobile traffic to a different target group.
explanation.why: NLB cannot inspect HTTP headers (Layer 4 only). NLB IP-based routing doesn't distinguish mobile vs desktop clients. ALB IP address rules don't help here — the distinction is in the User-Agent header.

questions.question: An ASG has minimum=2, desired=4, maximum=8. A target tracking policy targets 50% CPU. CPU drops to 10% for 15 minutes. What does the ASG do?

options.text: Immediately terminates all instances below minimum
Scales in, terminating instances until desired approaches minimum, but never below 2
Does nothing because CPU is still above 0%
Sets desired to 0 to save costs

explanation.correct: The ASG scales in (reduces instances) to maintain the 50% CPU target. It will reduce desired capacity, but it will never go below the minimum of 2 instances, regardless of how low CPU drops.
explanation.why: The minimum is a hard floor. The ASG termination happens gradually, not all at once. The ASG always responds to significant metric deviations. Desired can never go below minimum.

questions.question: What is the DEFAULT termination policy used by Auto Scaling Groups during scale-in events?

options.text: Newest instance first
Instance with most traffic
Oldest launch configuration first
Random selection

explanation.correct: The default ASG termination policy selects the instance with the oldest launch configuration (or launch template version) first, ensuring newer instances remain running.
explanation.why: Newest instance first is actually an available non-default policy. Traffic-based termination is not a built-in policy. Random selection would cause unpredictable behavior.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid chaining configuration between ALB and NLB?

options.text: ALB as frontend → NLB as backend target
NLB as frontend → ALB as backend target
ALB and NLB cannot be chained in any configuration
Both directions are equally supported

explanation.correct: NLB can have an ALB as a target. This pattern gives you a static Elastic IP (from NLB) plus intelligent HTTP routing (from ALB). The reverse — ALB targeting an NLB — is not supported.
explanation.why: ALB cannot forward to NLB as a target. They cannot be chained in both directions equally. The NLB → ALB pattern is a real production pattern used when clients need a static IP plus advanced routing.

questions.question: Your target group health check is configured to check /health every 30 seconds with a threshold of 3 failures before marking unhealthy. An instance goes down. How long before the ALB stops sending it traffic?

options.text: Immediately
30 seconds
90 seconds (3 failures × 30 seconds)
5 minutes

explanation.correct: With 3 consecutive failures required and 30-second intervals between checks, the instance must fail 3 checks before being marked unhealthy: 3 × 30 = 90 seconds minimum before traffic stops.
explanation.why: It is not immediate — health checks need time to confirm failure. One failed check (30s) is not enough. The threshold of 3 failures must be reached before the instance is marked unhealthy.

questions.question: An application uses WebSocket connections for real-time communication. Which load balancer is MOST appropriate and why?

options.text: NLB, because WebSocket uses TCP and NLB handles TCP best
ALB, because it natively supports WebSocket connections over HTTP/HTTPS
Either — both handle WebSocket identically
Neither — WebSocket requires a dedicated load balancer

explanation.correct: ALB provides native WebSocket support. WebSocket starts as an HTTP connection that is upgraded — since ALB understands HTTP (Layer 7), it handles this upgrade seamlessly and maintains the persistent connection.
explanation.why: While NLB can carry TCP traffic used by WebSocket, ALB's native HTTP upgrade handling makes it better suited. They do not handle WebSocket identically — ALB is explicitly designed for it.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'instance warm-up period' in an Auto Scaling Group scaling policy?

options.text: Time allowed for the instance to install software before receiving traffic
Time ASG waits before including a new instance's metrics in scaling calculations
Minimum uptime required before an instance can be terminated
Time allowed for health checks to complete

explanation.correct: The warm-up period tells ASG not to count a newly launched instance's metrics (e.g., CPU) in scaling decisions until it has had time to initialize. This prevents triggering another scale-out before the first new instance is ready.
explanation.why: Software installation is handled by user data before the instance is registered. Minimum uptime protection is instance scale-in protection, a different feature. Health check timing is separately configured.

questions.question: A listener rule has three path-based conditions with priorities 1, 2, and 3. An incoming request matches both priority 1 and priority 3 conditions. What happens?

options.text: Both rules are applied and the request goes to both target groups
The request goes to the target group of priority 3 (lowest priority wins)
The request goes to the target group of priority 1 (lowest number wins, evaluated first)
An error is returned because multiple rules matched

explanation.correct: ALB listener rules are evaluated in priority order. The lowest priority number is evaluated first. Once a matching rule is found, it is applied and evaluation stops — no further rules are checked.
explanation.why: Rules are not applied in combination. Higher priority number (3) is evaluated after lower number (1). AWS does not return errors for multiple matching rules — it simply applies the first match.

questions.question: A startup's architecture requires: static IP for firewall whitelisting, path-based routing to 5 microservices, and HTTPS termination. Design the optimal solution.

options.text: 5 separate NLBs with Elastic IPs, each serving one microservice
One ALB with Elastic IP assigned directly
One NLB with Elastic IP in front of one ALB configured with 5 path-based rules and HTTPS listener
5 separate ALBs with Route 53 routing

explanation.correct: NLB (with Elastic IP) → ALB (with HTTPS listener + 5 path rules) is the optimal pattern. NLB provides the static IP the firewall needs; ALB provides the intelligent HTTP routing. HTTPS is terminated at the ALB.
explanation.why: 5 NLBs would require 5 different IPs and cannot do path routing. ALB cannot directly hold an Elastic IP. 5 ALBs with Route 53 cannot do path routing either — Route 53 routes DNS, not HTTP paths.

questions.question: An Auto Scaling Group is attached to an ALB target group. During a scale-in event, ASG decides to terminate an instance. What happens to in-flight requests on that instance?

options.text: All in-flight requests are immediately dropped
The instance is deregistered first (connection draining), allowing in-flight requests to complete before termination
The ALB reroutes all in-flight requests to other targets immediately
The instance keeps running until all requests finish, regardless of ASG settings

explanation.correct: Before terminating an instance, ASG deregisters it from the target group. Connection draining (deregistration delay) allows existing connections to complete within a configurable timeout (default 300 seconds) before the instance is terminated.
explanation.why: Immediate drop would cause request failures. In-flight requests cannot be magically rerouted mid-connection. The instance does not stay running indefinitely — the deregistration delay has a timeout after which it terminates regardless.

questions.question: You need to implement canary deployments — route 5% of traffic to a new version of your application and 95% to the old version. Which ALB feature enables this?

options.text: Path-based routing with two separate paths
Weighted target groups — assigning weights within a single forwarding action
Two separate ALBs with Route 53 weighted routing
Health check manipulation to reduce traffic

explanation.correct: ALB supports weighted target groups in a single forwarding action. You set old-version TG weight=95 and new-version TG weight=5. ALB distributes traffic proportionally without needing separate load balancers.
explanation.why: Path-based routing routes 100% to one path — it cannot split a single path's traffic. Two ALBs work but are more complex and expensive. Health check manipulation is a hack, not a routing strategy.

questions.question: An NLB target group uses IP-based targets. A target IP is 10.0.1.50 on port 8080. Where can this IP reside?

options.text: Only within the same VPC as the NLB
Within the VPC, a peered VPC, on-premises via VPN or Direct Connect, or any routable IP
Only on EC2 instances
Only within the same Availability Zone as the NLB

explanation.correct: NLB IP-based targets support IPs anywhere that is routable: within the same VPC, a peered VPC, on-premises networks connected via VPN or Direct Connect, or any routable IP. This enables hybrid architectures.
explanation.why: ALB instance targets are VPC-scoped, but NLB IP targets are more flexible. On-premises server IPs are a primary use case for NLB IP targets via Direct Connect.

questions.question: Your ALB listener has path rules for /api, /web, and /admin. A request arrives for /dashboard which matches none of the rules. What happens?

options.text: The request is dropped silently
A 404 error is returned by the ALB
The default rule is applied (e.g., forward to default target group or return fixed response)
The request is forwarded to all target groups simultaneously

explanation.correct: Every ALB listener must have a default rule that handles requests matching no other rule. The default action can be: forward to a target group, return a fixed HTTP response, or redirect. The specific behavior depends on how the default rule was configured.
explanation.why: ALB never drops requests silently. The ALB itself does not generate 404s for unmatched paths — that's a default rule decision. Traffic is never duplicated to all target groups.

questions.question: Which scaling policy type uses machine learning to proactively scale BEFORE demand arrives?

options.text: Target Tracking Scaling
Step Scaling
Scheduled Scaling
Predictive Scaling

explanation.correct: Predictive Scaling uses machine learning to analyze historical traffic patterns and proactively scale out before demand hits, rather than reacting after metrics already spike.
explanation.why: Target tracking reacts to current metrics. Step scaling reacts to metric thresholds. Scheduled scaling uses fixed time schedules. Only Predictive Scaling is proactive using ML pattern analysis.

questions.question: A company runs a real-time multiplayer game using UDP protocol. Which load balancer should they use?

options.text: Application Load Balancer — because games are web applications
Network Load Balancer — because NLB supports UDP
Classic Load Balancer — for legacy game server support
ALB with WebSocket — because games use real-time connections

explanation.correct: NLB natively supports UDP protocol. Real-time multiplayer games commonly use UDP for low-latency data transfer where some packet loss is acceptable. NLB's ultra-low latency also makes it ideal for gaming.
explanation.why: ALB only supports HTTP, HTTPS, and WebSocket — not UDP. Classic Load Balancer is deprecated and should not be used for new workloads. WebSocket requires an HTTP upgrade which doesn't apply to UDP game traffic.

questions.question: You configure an ASG with desired=3 in us-east-1 across three AZs (us-east-1a, 1b, 1c). AZ 1b experiences an outage. How many instances will the ASG try to maintain and where?

options.text: 2 instances — one each in 1a and 1c
3 instances — ASG redistributes to maintain desired=3 across healthy AZs
1 instance — only the AZ that started the outage's instance is replaced
0 instances — ASG waits for 1b to recover

explanation.correct: ASG always tries to maintain the desired capacity. When 1b fails, ASG marks that instance unhealthy, launches a replacement, and attempts to distribute instances across available AZs (1a and 1c). Desired stays at 3.
explanation.why: ASG does not reduce desired capacity due to AZ failure — it rebalances. It does not wait for recovery. The replacement is for the desired count, not just the single failed instance.

questions.question: An ALB is configured with HTTPS listener on port 443. Traffic arrives on HTTP port 80. What rule would you configure to handle this elegantly without maintaining two separate backends?

options.text: Add HTTP:80 listener that forwards to the same target group as HTTPS
Add HTTP:80 listener with a redirect rule: HTTP → HTTPS (301 permanent redirect)
Disable port 80 — clients must use HTTPS directly
Use an NLB to handle port 80 and forward to the ALB

explanation.correct: The best practice is to add an HTTP:80 listener with a redirect action that sends all HTTP traffic to HTTPS with a 301 permanent redirect. This requires no backend changes and enforces HTTPS for all clients.
explanation.why: Forwarding HTTP to the same backend as HTTPS exposes your application over unencrypted HTTP. Disabling port 80 gives a poor user experience when users type the URL without https://. An NLB adds unnecessary complexity for this simple redirect use case.

questions.question: A developer asks: 'Can I attach the SAME EC2 instance to TWO different target groups on the SAME ALB?' What is the correct answer?

options.text: No — an EC2 instance can only be in one target group at a time
Yes — an EC2 instance can be registered in multiple target groups simultaneously
Yes, but only if the target groups use different ports
No — this would cause a routing loop

explanation.correct: An EC2 instance can be registered in multiple target groups simultaneously. The instance receives traffic for all target groups it belongs to. Health checks run independently per target group.
explanation.why: This is a valid architecture — for example, one instance serving both /api and /legacy paths. Port distinction is not required. No routing loop occurs because the ALB forwards to the instance, not back to itself.
